SolarSense — Solar Panel Performance Anomaly Detection¶

End-to-end prototype: synthetic data → weather-adjusted expected-generation model → anomaly detection → 7-day forecast → maintenance-priority dashboard¶

Problem: Solar installations silently lose output to soiling, shading, and inverter faults. Raw generation numbers are misleading because they're driven by weather. This notebook builds a weather-normalized expected vs. actual generation model, flags meaningful underperformance, classifies why (gradual decline vs. sudden fault), forecasts the next week, and ranks sites by estimated revenue impact.

1. Setup¶

2. Generate a synthetic dataset¶

Five sites, one year of daily data. Each site has a capacity (kW) and a "true" physical relationship between weather (irradiance, temperature, cloud cover) and generation. We then inject realistic faults into three of the five sites so the detection pipeline has something real to find:

Site Behavior
Site_A Healthy all year (control)
Site_B Healthy, then gradual soiling decline from day 200 onward (dust/debris buildup)
Site_C Healthy, then a sudden inverter fault on day 260, output collapses for ~18 days, then gets fixed
Site_D Healthy all year (control, different capacity)
Site_E Healthy, then partial shading appears from day 150 (new construction next door) — a smaller, steady drop 
(1825, 7)

3. Quick look at raw generation (weather noise makes faults hard to see by eye)¶

4. Build the weather-normalized "expected generation" baseline¶

For each site, we train a simple linear regression — generation ~ irradiance + temperature + cloud_cover — using only the first 90 days, which we treat as a known-healthy baseline period for every site (a real deployment would use a commissioning/warranty period, or the first few months post-install).

The model then predicts what generation should look like for the rest of the year given the actual weather that day. The gap between predicted and actual is the signal we care about.

R2 MAE_kwh
Site_A 0.99 3.07
Site_B 0.99 4.76
Site_C 0.99 3.93
Site_D 0.99 2.39
Site_E 0.99 6.47

6. Anomaly detection on the residuals¶

A single bad-weather day already gets absorbed by the regression, so we don't need to flag single-day dips. What matters is a sustained gap. We use a 7-day rolling average of the % gap and flag a day when:

  • the 7-day rolling gap is below -12% (meaningfully underperforming), and
  • it's stayed below that threshold for 3+ consecutive days (rules out noise)
site
Site_A      0
Site_B    125
Site_C     21
Site_D      0
Site_E    197
Name: flagged_days, dtype: int64

7. Classify why: gradual decline vs. sudden drop¶

The shape of the residual trend tells us which kind of problem it likely is:

  • Gradual: the rolling gap declines slowly over 30+ days → looks like soiling or shading buildup
  • Sudden: the rolling gap drops sharply within a 5-day window → looks like an inverter/wiring fault
Site_A               none
Site_B    gradual_decline
Site_C        sudden_drop
Site_D               none
Site_E    gradual_decline
Name: detected_pattern, dtype: str

8. Visualize expected vs. actual for every site, with flagged periods shaded¶

9. Estimate revenue impact and rank sites needing attention¶

Assume a simple electricity value of ₹6/kWh (adjustable). For each site, sum the shortfall (expected − actual) only on flagged days, and convert to an estimated ₹ loss. This lets maintenance teams prioritize by dollars, not just anomaly count.

priority_rank site detected_pattern flagged_days total_shortfall_kwh estimated_loss

1 2 Site_B gradual_decline 125 6,153.33 36,920.00
2 3 Site_C sudden_drop 21 2,074.58 12,447.00
3 4 Site_A none 0 -0.00 -0.00
4 5 Site_D none 0 -0.00 -0.00

10. 7-day forward forecast¶

Using each site's regression model plus the actual weather for the last 7 days of the dataset (standing in for a weather forecast feed in production), project expected generation for the coming week and compare it against how the site has actually been performing recently — giving an early "will this still be a problem next week" read.

site forecast_expected_avg_kwh recent_actual_avg_kwh recent_pct_gap currently_flagged

4 Site_E 156.46 135.71 -13.47 True

0 Site_A 77.88 76.78 -1.14 False

11. Maintenance-priority dashboard (single summary view)¶

12. Takeaways (what this demonstrates)¶

  • Site_A / Site_D stayed within normal weather-adjusted variance all year → correctly never flagged.
  • Site_B shows a slow-building gap from ~day 200 that our pattern classifier correctly labels gradual_decline → consistent with soiling, matches a maintenance-cleaning recommendation.
  • Site_C shows a sharp, short-lived collapse around day 260 correctly labeled sudden_drop → consistent with an inverter fault needing an urgent site visit.
  • Site_E's steady ~12% drop from day 150 gets picked up as sustained underperformance → consistent with new shading, worth an on-site inspection.
  • The priority dashboard turns this into a ranked, dollar-quantified maintenance queue instead of a wall of raw charts — exactly what an O&M team would act on.

This is intentionally built with simple, explainable methods (linear regression baseline + rolling-average threshold + slope-based classification) rather than a black-box model — in a real product this could be swapped for a more advanced model (e.g., gradient boosting, Prophet for the forecast) once there's enough real historical data per site.
